posts.caption:
You get 7 seconds to make a first impression and 30 to land your pitch.

Most people freeze or ramble. The fix is a formula: who you are, your proof, what you want, the hook back.

One number beats five adjectives every time.

Swipe for the formula and a worked example.

captionThread: You get 7 seconds to make a first impression and 30 to land your pitch. Most grads freeze or ramble. Here's the formula that fixes it. A thread.
The window: 7 seconds to a first impression, 30 seconds is the sweet spot for a pitch, and you're 3x more memorable if you lead with a result instead of a job title.
The formula, four parts in order. 1. Who you are: name + what you do, one line. 2. Your proof: one specific result. 3. What you want: be direct. 4. The hook back: end on a question.

What it sounds like: 'Hi, I'm Maya, I just finished a marketing degree. Last year I grew a festival's social from 2k to 15k followers in six months. I'm after a grad role in content. What does your team work on?'
Why it lands: a number they'll remember, a clear ask, and a question that hands them the mic. Read it aloud. If it runs long, cut the degree detail before you cut the result.
Flex it to the room: at a fair, lead with the ask. On a video call, keep it to 20 seconds. In a real lift, cut to proof plus ask. In a DM, same formula, written, under 90 words.

Cut these: the life story, the adjective pile, the mumbled ask, the 45-second monologue. Write your 4 parts, cut to 30 seconds, swap an adjective for a number, practise this week. www.internwise.co.uk

posts.title: Reading the Room in Interviews
posts.caption:
An interview is a two-way read. You're interviewing them too.

Green flags: they start selling the role, they ask what you'd want in year two, the time runs over.

Find roles at www.internwise.co.uk
captionThread: An interview is a two-way read. Most candidates only play one side. Here's how to spot the buying signals and the red flags. A thread.
Why it matters: the interview reads you AND you read them. 55% of a room's mood is body language, not words. One flag spotted early can save you months in the wrong job.
Green flags they want you: they shift from testing you to selling the role, they ask what you'd want in year two, the 30-min slot runs to 45, they pull in a colleague mid-interview.
Red flags to walk away: three people give three answers to 'what does success look like?', they dodge why the last person left, they pressure a yes on the spot, everyone in the room looks exhausted.

Live tells to read: leaning in means interest, match it. Checking the time means you're losing them, wrap up. Note-taking spikes mean you just landed something. Closed arms and short replies mean pivot to asking about them.
Questions that flip the table: 'What does success look like in the first 90 days?' 'Why did the last person leave?' 'What would you change about working here?' 'How's the team on a stressful week?'
Green: they sell, they linger, they introduce you. Red: no clear success, dodged turnover, rushed yes. Always ask the question that reads them back. www.internwise.co.uk

Move 1, buy time: 'Thank you, I'm really pleased. This is a big decision and I want to give it the attention it deserves. Could I come back to you by [date, 7-10 days out]?' 92% say yes.

Four fouls: bluffing an offer you don't have, accepting then reneging, playing them against each other, deciding on salary alone. The £5K gap disappears in year 2. The learning gap compounds for a decade.

captionThread: The average UK Glassdoor rating is 3.4 and it tells you nothing. 71% of reviews come from people on their way out. Four better sources, 20 minutes, all public. A thread.
Why reviews are the worst source: 3.4 is the average across all UK employers. 71% of reviews are written by leavers or recent leavers. You're reading a exit-interview sample, not a culture.

Source A, their last 6 job ads. Free on their careers page. Which teams are hiring tells you where the money is. The same role posted twice in 6 months means someone left. Three times means a manager problem.
Source B, LinkedIn tenure math. Filter their people by your target team and read the start dates. Nobody past 2 years is the loudest signal on this list. Ask about it in the interview.
Source C, Companies House. Free and public. Filed accounts, director changes, charges. Late filings plus sudden director resignations, together, are the pattern to watch. Both are timestamped.
Source D, their eng or product blog. Read the last three posts. You learn their stack, their problems, and their taste. Nothing published in 2 years is itself worth knowing.
Twenty minutes across four free sources. Then walk into the interview knowing more than the other candidates. All of it is public. www.internwise.co.uk

captionThread: 90% of grad first rounds are now video. And recruiters decide in the first 7 seconds. Here's how to nail those seconds - the room, the opening, the body language. A thread.
The data: 90% of grad first-rounds are video. 7 seconds is the decision window. 55% of that first impression is body language and setting, not your words. Your setup does half the work.
The 5 setup rules: camera at eye level (stack books). Light in front, never behind. Neutral background. Wired ethernet if possible. Wired headphones - AirPods die at the worst moment.
Your first 60 seconds: smile 3 seconds before you unmute. Thank them by name. Then reference one thing about the company - a launch, campaign, or announcement. Warm. Human. Prepared.
Body language wins: look at the camera not the screen. Nod slowly. Keep hands visible. Lean 5cm forward when engaged. Don't read from notes, don't cross arms, don't look at your own tile.
When tech dies: if they freeze, wait 10 seconds before repeating. If audio dies, dial in by phone. If a housemate walks in, pause calmly and return. Composure wins the moment.
Practice. Then practice again. Record yourself. Rewatch on mute - is your body open? Do a full run 24h before the real thing. Find roles worth interviewing for at www.internwise.co.uk

posts.title: STAR Method for Behavioural Interviews
posts.caption:
Every behavioural interview question is asking for the same thing: a clear story.

Situation. Task. Action. Result.

Four parts. Four sentences. The interviewer stays with you the whole way.

Swipe for the exact structure and 3 stories every grad should have ready.

Find interviews worth prepping for at www.internwise.co.uk
captionThread: Every 'tell me about a time...' question is asking for the same thing: a clear story in a clear shape. STAR is that shape. A thread on how to use it without sounding robotic.

Without structure: 'Well, so basically in second year, before that I did this thing, and there was a project, kind of...' With STAR: four sentences, clear beginning, clear end. Interviewers score you higher on communication.
S = Situation. One sentence. Where, when, what team. Skip the backstory of the backstory. 15 seconds of context is enough.
T = Task. What YOU needed to do. Make your role obvious, not the team's. This is where interviewers separate you from the group.
A = Action. 60% of your answer lives here. Use 'I' not 'we'. Every sentence. Show judgment, not just activity.
R = Result. Numbers, always numbers. Even rough estimates land. Tie it back to the task. End with what you learned - shows self-awareness.
3 stories every grad needs ready: a time you led something, a time you handled conflict, a time you failed and learned. Drill them into STAR shape. Find interviews at www.internwise.co.uk

posts.title: Your First 30 Days
posts.caption:
The first 30 days at a new job shape how they see you for the first year.

Most people spend them trying not to make mistakes. The smart ones spend them building visibility.

Here's the playbook.

www.internwise.co.uk
captionThread: The first 30 days at a new job shape how they see you for the first year. Here's the playbook for getting it right from day one. A thread.
Week 1 rule: listen more than you speak. Observe the culture before you comment on it. Learn the names. Understand the politics. Ask questions. Don't have opinions yet.
Week 2 goal: pick one visible task and deliver it cleanly. Doesn't need to be big. Needs to be on time and well-communicated. Reliability compounds.
Week 3 move: schedule a coffee chat with someone outside your direct team. One conversation builds more goodwill than a month of desk work.

Source: Staffing Industry Analysts.

posts.title: Iced Coffee Stirs Job Interview Debate
posts.caption:
A Guardian article picked up a debate that started online: is it unprofessional to arrive at a job interview holding an iced coffee?

The real story is not the drink. It is how small signals get judged in interviews, especially when the candidate is early in their career. Some hiring managers may read a takeaway cup as too casual. Others may see that reaction as outdated, because it says little about whether someone can actually do the job.

For students and graduates, the useful lesson is this: interviews still come with unwritten rules. You do not need to become robotic, but you do need to think about the first impression you are creating before the first question is asked.

Practical takeaway: keep the focus on your preparation, examples, and fit for the role. If something might distract the interviewer before you have made your case, leave it outside the room.

Source: The Guardian.

Source: BBC Business.

posts.title: Your First-Day Intro, Sorted
posts.caption:
Starting an internship can be nerve-wracking, but introducing yourself doesn’t have to be! Here’s a simple way to make a memorable first impression:

1. Say your name, your role, and how long you’ll be with the team. 
2. Add a line about what you’re studying or an interest you have. This adds a personal touch.
3. Ask a question about their work. Being curious shows you’re engaged and ready to learn.
4. Listen. It’s not just about speaking; absorbing information is key.
5. At the end of the day, send a brief message to your manager thanking them for the welcome. It shows professionalism and gratitude.

Remember, your introduction sets the tone for your time there. So go on, make it count! Learn more about making the most of your internship at www.internwise.co.uk

posts.title: Fake Job Interviews Used in Crypto Heist
posts.caption:
An alarming incident has emerged in the job market. A major cryptocurrency exchange disclosed a $6.3 billion hack engineered through fake job interviews. An engineer, contacted via a legitimate job-hunting platform, was led into a trap with phony interviews conducted by impostors posing as company representatives.

This situation underscores the increasing risks present in online job-seeking environments. For students and graduates embarking on their career journeys, it's essential to remain cautious and verify the legitimacy of job offers and interviews. Even when approached through well-known platforms, double-checking the credentials of potential employers can prevent falling victim to scams.

Internships stand out as a safer alternative. By engaging with verified companies, they provide a genuine avenue to develop professional skills and gain industry insights, all while safeguarding against fraudulent activities. Internwise is committed to connecting you with trustworthy opportunities. Stay informed and make informed decisions. Source: BBC Business.

posts.title: How Many Hours Can You Work?
posts.caption: When an application asks how many hours you're available to work, it's crucial to answer honestly and specifically. Don’t just say you're flexible. If you can manage 15 to 20 hours a week, say so. Mention the days or times you can work, especially if you have lectures to plan around. Try to match the job advert's expectations - full-time roles usually mean 35 to 40 hours. If you're on a Student visa, remember degree-level students can often work up to 20 hours a week in term time. Never promise more hours than you can commit to - it’s the quickest way to lose a good role. Be clear, be honest, and set yourself up for success. Check out www.internwise.co.uk for more tips.
